reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO nutrition guidance
clinicalPearls: Classically causes a macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia, but neurological features can appear before anaemia and even with normal blood counts
Subacute combined degeneration of the cord produces symmetrical distal paraesthesiae, loss of proprioception and vibration sense, and an unsteady gait
Autoimmune loss of gastric intrinsic factor (pernicious anaemia) and prior gastric or terminal ileal surgery are common mechanisms of malabsorption
Strict vegetarian and vegan diets, common in parts of India, are an important dietary cause because the vitamin is almost exclusively of animal origin
A blood film may show oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils; marrow is megaloblastic
Serum cobalamin can be borderline, so raised methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are useful confirmatory markers
Replacement reverses the anaemia reliably, but longstanding neurological damage may only partially recover, making early treatment important
Correcting B12 with folate alone can precipitate or worsen neurological deterioration, so B12 status must be assessed before treating a megaloblastic anaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Cobalamin is a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Deficiency impairs conversion of homocysteine to methionine and of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, disrupting DNA synthesis and myelin maintenance. Impaired DNA synthesis in haematopoietic precursors yields megaloblastic, ineffective erythropoiesis, while disordered myelin metabolism underlies the neuropathy and cord degeneration. Absorption depends on intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells and an intact terminal ileum, so autoimmune gastritis, atrophic gastritis, gastric or ileal resection, and malabsorptive states all reduce uptake; dietary lack occurs when animal products are excluded.
additionalDifferentials: Folate deficiency (other cause of megaloblastic anaemia)
Other causes of peripheral neuropathy such as diabetes
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film for macrocytosis and hypersegmented neutrophils
Serum cobalamin, with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine when the level is equivocal
Anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies for pernicious anaemia
Reticulocyte count and haemolysis markers as ineffective erythropoiesis can raise LDH and bilirubin
Assessment for malabsorption and coexisting iron or folate deficiency
redFlags: Progressive myelopathy or gait disturbance indicating subacute combined degeneration needing urgent treatment
Cognitive decline or psychiatric change attributable to deficiency
Pancytopenia from profound megaloblastic marrow failure
reference.prognosis: Haematological recovery is usually complete with replacement, but neurological recovery depends on how long deficiency was present; early treatment gives the best outcome while advanced cord degeneration may leave residual deficits.
pitfalls: Treating megaloblastic anaemia with folate alone and masking or worsening B12-related neurological disease
Attributing neurological symptoms to another cause because the blood count is normal
Relying solely on a borderline serum cobalamin without functional markers
Failing to identify and monitor pernicious anaemia and its association with other autoimmune disease and gastric cancer
